The Bible stands out by several verifiable traits: it is *historical* (anchored in places, kings, and events corroborated by archaeology), *prophetic* (precise predictions fulfilled), *unique in its message* (a God who comes to save freely, when other systems say "do enough works"), and *Christocentric* (it culminates in a Person, Jesus, whose resurrection is a fact to examine).

The best judge is not the label "religious": it is the content. Compare honestly what each says about God, humanity, evil, and salvation. Jesus prayed this way: "Sanctify them by the truth; your word is truth." Truth has no fear of comparison; it invites it.
items.evidence: Unlike texts founded on the private visions of a single man, Christian faith rests on *public* events, situated in history and verifiable (crucifixion under Pilate, empty tomb, multiple witnesses). It is a radically different type of foundation, one that exposes itself to historical examination rather than avoiding it.

items.q: How do I memorize and meditate on the Word?
items.a:
To memorize and meditate on the Word is to move it from the page to your heart, so it dwells in you. "I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you." A memorized verse is a resource available everywhere — in temptation, anxiety, at night — when you don't have your Bible at hand.

To *memorize*, something concrete: choose *one* verse that speaks to you, write it down, repeat it aloud several times a day, connect it to a moment (your coffee, your commute), and review older ones. One verse per week, kept consistently, gives you 50 verses in a year.

*Meditation* is not "clearing your mind" (as in other spiritualities), but "filling" it: slowly savoring a text, like sucking on candy to draw out all its flavor. Read it slowly, dwell on each word, ask questions ("What does this say about God? about me?"), pray it and let it work. "Blessed is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night... Whatever they do prospers."
items.evidence: Biblical meditation differs fundamentally from meditations aimed at "emptying" the mind: it *fills* it with specific content. Cognitive science also confirms the effectiveness of spaced repetition and association for anchoring a text permanently — exactly the means biblical tradition has employed since ancient times.

items.q: Should I read the Bible every day?
items.a:
"Should" sounds like an obligation; let's see it rather as a vital need and a privilege. Jesus says: "Man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God." The Word is to your soul what food is to your body: skipping meals weakens you.

Why *every* day? Because relationship, like appetite, is lived in the present. You don't eat for a whole week at once. A daily time, even brief, reconnects you to God, orients your day, refreshes your spirit, and keeps you. The first Christians "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching": consistency, not occasional intensity, fosters growth.

But flee guilt and legalism. If you miss a day, God loves you no less — simply resume, without condemning yourself. Aim for your heart, not performance: five minutes of savored, prayed meditation beats thirty read mechanically. Make it a joyful appointment with someone you love, not a box to check.
items.evidence: The parallel between food and Word (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4) illuminates the recommended regularity: this is not a religious rule, but a need. The constant experience of believers — like the logic of any relationship or learning — confirms that daily contact, even brief, bears more fruit than intense, scattered effort.

items.q: Why does God allow suffering?
items.a:
It is the most honest question there is, and the Bible never evades it. Much evil comes from human freedom misused (wars, injustice, selfishness), and some from a broken world, "subject to decay." God did not create suffering; He even declared it an enemy, and He came to defeat it.

What is unique about Christian faith is that God does not explain suffering *from a distance*: He enters *into* it. In Jesus, He hungered, wept, was betrayed, was tortured. He does not watch your suffering from on high; He suffered with you and for you. The cross is proof that a good God can be present at the very heart of pain.

He wastes nothing: "In all things God works for the good of those who love him." That does not mean everything *is* good, but that He can draw good even from what breaks you — often by transforming your wounds into compassion for others. And He promises an end to it all: one day, He "will wipe every tear from their eyes."
items.evidence: The problem of evil reverses into an argument: to call something "unjust," you need a standard of justice that transcends our opinions. Without God, nothing remains but an indifferent universe where the word "evil" loses its meaning. This is the reasoning that moved C. S. Lewis from atheism to faith.

items.q: I have doubts. Is that serious?
items.a:
No, doubt is not a sin or the death of faith — it is often a sign that your faith is alive and seeking. The Bible is full of believers who doubted: John the Baptist in prison, Thomas at the tomb, David in the Psalms. None was rejected; Jesus met them with patience.

There are, in fact, two kinds of doubt. Doubt *that seeks* ("Help me believe!") moves toward God and lets itself be answered. Doubt *that flees* (looking for excuses not to commit) moves away. Bring your questions to God rather than distance yourself from Him: "Come now, let us settle the matter, says the Lord." He is not afraid of your "whys."

What to do concretely? Be honest (with God and with a mature Christian), seek answers (faith has good reasons), and do not cut yourself off from the means of grace even when you don't "feel" anything. Thomas doubted — then, met by Jesus, he made one of the most beautiful confessions: "My Lord and my God!" Doubt traversed can become deeper faith.
items.evidence: A striking fact: the Gospels do not erase the disciples' doubts, even after the resurrection (Matthew 28:17). This embarrassing honesty is a mark of authenticity — and an encouragement: biblical faith does not require the absence of questions, but the willingness to carry them to God.

items.q: Does God hear me when I pray and nothing changes?
items.a:
This feeling is one of the harshest trials, and the Bible gives it legitimacy: half the Psalms are cries from people who pray without seeing an answer ("How long, Lord?"). That God had these prayers recorded tells you that He *hears* even the cry that doubts being heard.

Silence is not absence. God answers, but not always with the change we demand: sometimes "not yet," sometimes "I have something better," sometimes by changing *us* rather than the situation. "The Lord is close to the brokenhearted." His closeness is promised even — especially — when nothing moves on the outside.

Keep praying with honesty, without pretending. Tell Him your disappointment; lay down your burden ("Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you"). And surround yourself: God often comforts through other believers. The apparent silence sometimes works in depth a trust that no longer depends on circumstances.
items.evidence: The massive presence of "lament psalms" in the Bible (nearly a third of the Psalter) is unique among religious books: it validates the believer's complaint instead of censoring it. Far from denial, biblical faith integrates the unanswered cry — a sign of its realism.

items.q: How do I walk through grief, the loss of a loved one?
items.a:
Grief is one of the deepest pains, and faith does not ask you to pretend to be fine. Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of His friend Lazarus ("Jesus wept") — God does not despise your tears; He shares them. Weeping is not lack of faith.

But the Christian does not weep "like the rest of mankind, who have no hope." For the one who is in Christ, death is not a wall but a passage: "Away from the body and at home with the Lord." The separation is real and painful, but it is not final — the resurrection promises reunion.

Meanwhile, let God carry you: "The Lord is close to the brokenhearted." Allow yourself to move through the waves of sorrow without guilt, lean on the presence of others, and speak to God about your pain. Healing is slow; He does not rush you. "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes" — one day, there will be "no more mourning."
items.evidence: Christian hope in the face of death does not deny pain but walks through it differently: studies on grief show that solid hope and a supporting community favor better passage through sorrow. Faith does not anesthetize pain — it gives it a horizon.

items.q: Where is God when everything collapses?
items.a:
When everything collapses, the question "Where is God?" is not blasphemy: it is the cry of faith seeking. And the Bible's answer is not a theory, but a presence: "God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble." He is not *above* the storm; He is *in* it, with you.

Often you don't *feel* this presence in the moment — but it does not depend on feelings. "Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for *you are with me*." Notice: the shepherd does not make the sheep avoid the valley; he walks *through it with* her.

And look at the cross: at the darkest moment of suffering, when Jesus cried out "Why have you forsaken me?", God was actually accomplishing our salvation. What you take for absence may be invisible work in progress. Keep holding to Him in the dark — many testify to having met Him most really at the bottom of the abyss.
items.evidence: The recurring testimony of those who have walked through extreme traumas (bereavements, camps, illnesses) is striking: many of them describe, not God's absence, but a presence particularly real "at the bottom." This paradox — God close precisely in collapse — runs through all Christian spiritual history.

items.q: Why do the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer?
items.a:
It is a scandal that the Bible faces head-on — an entire psalm (73) is devoted to it: "My feet had almost slipped; I had nearly lost my foothold. For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked." Your outrage is therefore legitimate and biblical; God does not reprove you for feeling it.

The key arrives when the psalmist "enters the sanctuary of God" and considers the *end*: the prosperity of the wicked is real but short; the account is not yet settled. We judge the snapshot; God sees the whole story. "Do not fret... for the wicked will be cut down like grass." Justice delayed is not justice denied.

Two things help. First, the assurance that there will be fair judgment: "God will repay each person according to what they have done." Second, a change of desire: the psalm ends not with revenge, but with "Whom have I in heaven but you?" The truly happy life was not in what the wicked had, but in God Himself. The believer apparently "losing" already possesses what matters most.
items.evidence: Psalm 73 is a model of honesty: it exposes the temptation (apparent injustice) *before* resolving it. This structure — plainly posing the scandal, then illuminating it through the perspective of eternity — shows a faith that does not flee reality but walks through it with clarity.

items.q: I feel unworthy and ashamed. What do I do?
items.a:
Shame locks you up, but God wants to set you free. First, you need to distinguish between two voices. *Guilt* says "I did something wrong" and can lead to forgiveness; *shame* says "I *am* bad, worthless" — and that doesn't come from God, but from the accuser who wants to separate you from him.

Here's the truth that breaks shame: "There is now no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ." In Christ, your worth doesn't depend on your achievements or your past, but on his love: you are "bought at a great price," called a child of God. He doesn't define you by the worst of what you've done, but by what Jesus did for you.

Practically: bring him what weighs on you (forgiveness dissolves real guilt), replace shame's lies with what God says about you (reread verses about your identity), and don't stay alone with it. Shame loses its power in the light and in relationship. You are not worthless: you are loved, forgiven, restored.
items.evidence: Psychology clearly distinguishes guilt ("I acted wrongly," which can be reparative) and shame ("I am bad," toxic and paralyzing) — a distinction the Bible has made all along. The message of a worth *received*, independent of performance, is recognized as a powerful remedy for shame.

items.q: How do I overcome anxiety and fear?
items.a:
Anxiety is an immense and very common struggle — and the Bible addresses it with compassion, not reproach. "Do not be anxious about anything" is not a guilt-inducing command, but an invitation to exchange: where you carry a burden alone, God offers to carry it with you.

Paul's "recipe" is concrete: "In everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts." Three actions: *name* your fear precisely before God, *give thanks* for what is going well (this shifts your focus), and *release* — "Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you."

Add practical supports: come back to the present (Jesus: "Each day has enough trouble of its own"), feed your mind with what is "true, noble, pure," surround yourself with others, and remember that getting help (doctor, therapist) is not a lack of faith. The peace promised is not the absence of the storm, but an inner guard in the midst of it.
items.evidence: Recognized approaches to anxiety (refocusing on the present, gratitude, reorienting thoughts, social support, expressing emotions) remarkably overlap with biblical wisdom (Matthew 6:34; Philippians 4:6-8). Prayer and professional help don't oppose each other — they complement each other.

items.q: Is God angry with me when I suffer?
items.a:
No — that's a stubborn lie that makes pain worse. Suffering is not proof of God's anger toward you. The cross settled this question once and for all: all the anger owed for our faults fell on Jesus, "the punishment that brought us peace was on him." For the child of God, there remains no condemnation.

The Bible instead shows faithful and *beloved* servants who suffered greatly: Job ("a righteous man"), Joseph, Paul, Jesus himself. Suffering, therefore, is not a sign of disgrace. Sometimes God disciplines (as a loving father, never as an avenging judge — "the Lord disciplines the one he loves"), but most often pain simply comes from a broken world.

What God guarantees you in trial is not his anger, but his faithfulness: "Mountains may depart and hills may crumble, but my loving devotion will never leave you." Don't read your suffering as rejection: read it in the light of the cross, which proves once and for all which side God is on — yours.
items.evidence: The book of Job exists precisely to dismantle the idea "you suffer, so God is against you": Job's friends defend this thesis… and God declares them *wrong* (Job 42:7). The Bible itself explicitly refutes the automatic link between suffering and divine anger.

items.q: How do I forgive someone who hurt me deeply?
items.a:
Forgiving a deep wound is one of the hardest things there is — and the Bible doesn't take it lightly. First, let's clarify what forgiveness *isn't*: it's not excusing the wrong ("it doesn't matter"), not forgetting, not necessarily returning to danger with the offender. It's giving up revenge and placing the debt in the hands of the righteous Judge.

Why do it? Not because the other person deserves it, but because holding a grudge chains you to your wound and poisons you. Forgiveness is first a liberation for the victim. And it draws its strength from its source: "Forgive each other, just as in Christ God forgave you." We forgive because we ourselves were first forgiven enormously.

It's a process, not a switch. It often begins with a decision ("I choose not to demand revenge") long before emotions follow, and it can replay each time the pain rises again. Give your anger to God, ask him for the strength you don't have, and move forward step by step. Forgiving doesn't mean it was nothing; it means you entrust justice to God and you choose to be free.
items.evidence: Many studies in psychology link forgiveness to better mental and physical health (lower anxiety, depression, blood pressure), while holding grudges sustains stress. What the Bible presents as a liberating command is thus verified in the facts.

items.q: Why does my prayer seem to go unanswered?
items.a:
A prayer with "no answer" rarely is in the strict sense: God always responds, but sometimes with "no," "not yet," or "I have something better" — like a good father who doesn't grant *every* request from his child, precisely because he loves him and sees further.

Several reasons can be at play, without guilt: the *timing* (God prepares, matures — "there is a time for everything"), a *greater good* we don't yet see, or an answer *different* from what we expected (Paul asks for his hardship to be removed; God gives him grace instead). Sometimes the waiting itself forges in us trust and perseverance.

Jesus tells a parable on purpose "to show that they should always pray and not give up." So: keep praying, be honest about your disappointment, but stay confident. And remember that the first purpose of prayer is not to get things, but to stay connected to the One who loves you — and *that* answer, his presence, is never refused.
items.evidence: Paul's case (2 Corinthians 12:8-9) — three prayers to be freed from his hardship, and a "no" paired with greater grace — sets the benchmark: the absence of the requested answer is not the absence of an answer. Prayer in the Bible transforms the one praying as much as the circumstances.

items.q: Suicide, depression: what does faith say?
items.a:
This subject calls for immense gentleness: if you're going through this, know first that your suffering is real, that you're not "less of a believer" for experiencing it, and that your life has infinite worth in God's eyes. Depression is not a sin or a lack of faith — it's an illness that touches even faithful believers (Elijah wanted to die; David knew the abyss).

The Bible doesn't condemn those who suffer this way; it surrounds them. "The Lord is near to those who have a broken heart." Nothing — "neither death nor life, nor the depths" — can separate you from his love. Even when you feel nothing, he won't let go of you: "If I go down to the realm of the dead, you are there."

Very practically: talk — to God, but also to someone close and to a professional (doctor, psychologist). Getting help is not a lack of faith: it's wisdom, and God heals through care too. If you have suicidal thoughts, don't stay alone for another second: call a helpline or emergency services now. Your life matters, you are loved, and there is a way out of this dark pit — even if you can't see it yet.
items.evidence: The Bible depicts without reserve the distress of great believers (Elijah in 1 Kings 19, Job, many psalms), which dismantles the false idea "a true believer never gets depressed." Current approaches insist, like faith, on *breaking isolation* and *seeking help* — absolute priority in case of suicidal thoughts (in the US, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline: 988).

items.q: How do I know God's will for my life?
items.a:
God's will is less a "hidden plan" to guess than a path to walk with him. The Bible distinguishes two levels. His *revealed* will — what he wants for everyone — is already clear in Scripture: that you know him, that you become like Jesus, that you love, that you live in holiness ("God's will is for you to be sanctified"). The essentials are already written.

For his *particular* will (career, marriage, life choices), God guides the one already walking with him: "Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God's will is." A renewed heart learns to perceive what pleases God.

Practically, cross-check several compasses: Scripture (nothing against it), prayer and inner peace, wisdom and common sense, counsel from mature believers, your gifts and deep desires ("he will give you the desires of your heart" when you make your delight in him), and circumstances. Often, God's will is discovered *by walking*, one obedient step at a time, more than by waiting for a spectacular sign.
items.evidence: The Bible emphasizes, not a "secret plan" to decode, but a character to become and a relationship to live (1 Thessalonians 4:3; Micah 6:8). This approach frees you from the anxiety of "what if I miss THE plan?": God actively guides the one walking with him; he doesn't trap you.

items.q: I keep falling back into the same sins. What do I do?
items.a:
Every believer knows this struggle — even Paul describes it: "The good I want to do, I do not do." You're therefore not alone, not abnormal, not a "fake Christian." But God offers more than resignation: a path to progressive victory.

A few keys. First, don't fight alone and by willpower alone: ask for the Holy Spirit's power ("Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh"). Next, attack the *triggers* upstream ("Do not think about how to satisfy your sinful desires") — cut off occasions, entry points. Then, step out of the shadows: hidden sin feeds on secrecy; "confess your sins to each other… so that you may be healed." A trusted brother or sister changes everything.

Finally, don't confuse *falling* with *identity*: when you stumble, get up quickly without drowning in shame ("there is no condemnation"), confess, and move on. Holiness is built by repeated returns to grace, not by instant perfection. "He will strengthen you to the end."
items.evidence: Habit science confirms biblical strategy: act on *triggers* and environment, give account to someone, replace the behavior rather than just forbid it. Fighting relapse succeeds better in community than in isolation — exactly what James 5:16 recommends.

items.q: Do I need the church, or can I believe alone?
items.a:
You can believe alone, but you're not *made* to live faith alone — and it impoverishes you. The Bible compares believers to a *body*: "You are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it." A limb cut off from the body shrivels; a coal pulled from the fire dies out fast.

The Church isn't first a building or a performance, but a family where you bear one another up: "Let us not abandon our meeting together… but encourage one another." You receive teaching, encouragement, prayer, the gifts of others there, and you give in turn. Many commands in the New Testament ("love one another," "carry each other's burdens") are simply *impossible* to live out alone.

If the Church has disappointed or hurt you — that happens, because it's made of imperfect humans — don't give up on communion itself: find a healthy community, centered on Jesus and his Word. You don't need a perfect Church, but a family to grow in. We thrive together more than alone.
items.evidence: The image of the "body" (1 Corinthians 12) implies interdependence: no member is self-sufficient. On the human level too, belonging to a caring community is one of the factors most strongly linked to well-being and perseverance over time — isolated faith erodes faster.

items.q: How do I resist temptation?
items.a:
Temptation itself isn't sin: Jesus was tempted without ever sinning. Sin begins when you give in. So don't condemn yourself for *being* tempted; the struggle is the sign that you're moving against the current, not that you're already lost.

Good news: "God will not allow you to be tempted beyond your ability to bear it; with every temptation he will also provide a way out." There's always an exit — you just have to take it quickly. Like Joseph facing temptation, sometimes wisdom is simply to *flee*, not to negotiate.

Concrete weapons: *Scripture* (Jesus answered the tempter "it is written…" — memorize verses), *prayer* ("watch and pray so that you will not fall into temptation"), *cutting off occasions* beforehand, and *not staying alone* with the struggle. Finally, replace: you don't chase out emptiness; you fill it with something better — communion with God and good desires. Victory isn't the absence of temptation, but the habit of getting out of it.
items.evidence: Jesus's strategy in the wilderness (answering with Scripture, refusing to enter into dialogue) and Joseph's strategy (fleeing, Genesis 39) align with what we know about self-control: avoiding prolonged exposure to temptation is far more effective than resisting it 'by willpower' once you're already in it.

items.q: Should I give a tithe? What does the Bible say about money?
items.a:
The Bible says much about money — not to guilt you, but because the way we handle it reveals our hearts ("where your treasure is, there your heart will be also"). Basic principle: everything belongs to God, and we are stewards, not owners.

Tithing (giving 10%) comes from the Old Testament and remains an excellent guideline for learning to give with priority and confidence. But the New Testament shifts the emphasis from the *rule* to the *heart*: "Let each one give as he has purposed in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver." The important thing isn't reaching a percentage reluctantly, but giving generously, freely, regularly.

Beyond giving, the Bible invites wisdom (avoiding debt that enslaves, saving, working honestly) and especially freedom from money: "the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil." The aim isn't to despise money, but to master it instead of being enslaved by it — and to discover that "it is more blessed to give than to receive."
items.evidence: Planned and joyful generosity is a proven antidote to money's grip: studies link regular giving to greater well-being and less financial anxiety. The Bible has always connected generosity with inner freedom (Acts 20:35) — a link contemporary research confirms.

items.q: How do I hear God's voice for my decisions?
items.a:
God doesn't want to leave you in the dark about your decisions; he promises to guide those who lean on him: "Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight." The condition is trust and listening, not the certainty of hearing an audible voice.

Cross-check multiple sources — God loves to confirm. *Scripture* first (he will never lead you against it); *prayer and inner peace* ("let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts"); *wisdom* and common sense (God has given you a mind); *counsel* from mature believers ("in the abundance of counselors there is safety"); *circumstances* and open or closed doors; and your *gifts and deep desires*.

For small decisions, move forward with wisdom and peace without over-spiritualizing everything. For big ones, take time, fast and pray if needed, and seek confirmation. And remember: God cares more about *who you become* than getting every detail "perfectly." Walk with him, and he will straighten your paths along the way.
items.evidence: The convergence of several "compasses" (Scripture, peace, counsel, circumstances, wisdom) is the method you find throughout Acts, including for major decisions (Acts 15: prayer, debate, Scripture, consensus). This approach protects against impulsive choices based on a single uncertain "sign."

items.q: What is fasting, and why do it?
items.a:
Fasting is voluntarily going without food (or something else) for a time in order to devote yourself more fully to God. It's not a hunger strike to "force" God, nor a religious achievement: it's saying, with your body, "I hunger for you more than for bread." Jesus assumes it's normal: "*When* you fast..." — not "if."\n\nWhy do it? To intensify prayer and listening, express your dependence, humble yourself before God, seek direction or a breakthrough, master your appetites. In Scripture, fasting often accompanies major turning points (Ezra, Esther, the church at Antioch before sending missionaries). The energy and time "gained" are transformed into prayer.

How? Simply and wisely: start small (one meal, one day), replace that time with prayer and God's Word, drink water, and adapt to your health (be careful with medical issues or pregnancy...). Jesus warns against fasting "to be seen": do it quietly, for God alone, and "your Father who sees in secret will reward you." The goal isn't performance, but a renewed hunger for God.
items.evidence: Fasting is a universal practice across great traditions, and medicine recognizes certain benefits of structured fasting. But its biblical value is first *relational*: Jesus assumes it (Matthew 6:16), without making it a merit — the emphasis falls on discretion and heart, not on achievement.

items.q: How do I share my faith without being pushy?
items.a:
Sharing your faith isn't "selling" a product or winning a debate: it's talking about a person you love. The foundation is first *your life*: "let your light shine before men." A transformed, loving, peaceful life raises questions — and then "always be ready to give a reason for your hope... but with gentleness and respect." Gentleness and respect: your tone matters as much as your content.

The best "tool" is your own testimony: simply tell what God has changed in you. You can argue a doctrine, but hardly a lived story ("I was blind, now I see"). Listen first, truly care about people, answer *their* questions rather than imposing a speech. Genuine love is never "pushy."\n\nFinally, remember you don't convert anyone — the Spirit touches hearts; you plant and love. That takes all the pressure off: be faithful, patient, natural, and pray for your loved ones. One right word, an attitude, an invitation at the right moment is worth more than ten arguments thrown at someone. "One plants, another waters, but God makes it grow."
items.evidence: Research on conversion journeys shows that most people approach faith through a *relationship* of trust and a lived testimony, far more than through an argument or pressure. The biblical counsel — consistent life, listening, gentleness, respect (1 Peter 3:15) — matches exactly what "works" humanly.

items.q: How do I handle anger and conflict?
items.a:
Anger is not in itself a sin — Jesus grew angry at injustice. The Bible says: "Be angry and sin not; do not let the sun go down on your wrath." The problem isn't *feeling* anger, but letting it lead you into evil or festering into bitterness.

A few principles. *Slow down*: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." A moment of pause avoids much damage. *Address the issue, not the person*: seek to resolve, not to wound or win. *Speak truth with gentleness*: "a soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger." *Don't let it linger*: settle quickly, before the wound festers into bitterness.

For conflicts, Jesus gives a roadmap: go first and see the person alone, in humility ("first remove the plank from your own eye"), seek reconciliation more than victory. Hand your anger to God, ask him for a peaceful heart, and remember the goal: "as much as is possible, live peaceably with all." Peace isn't avoiding conflict, but going through it in love.
items.evidence: Research on conflict management echoes biblical wisdom: pause before reacting, address the problem not the person, use a gentle tone, and don't let resentments pile up. "Do not let the sun go down on your wrath" (Ephesians 4:26) sums up a proven principle: don't let bitterness stew.

items.q: What does the Bible say about relationships, marriage, and singleness?
items.a:
The Bible holds both marriage and singleness in high honor, not as opposites. Marriage, established by God at creation, is the union of a man and a woman, called to become "one flesh": a covenant of faithful, exclusive, lasting love, an image of Christ's love for the church (Ephesians 5). It's not just a contract, but a sacred commitment made to endure.

It therefore calls us to protect this union: fidelity, love that gives itself ("husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church"), mutual respect, daily forgiveness. And it reserves sexual intimacy to this covenant — not from distrust of the body (which it celebrates, see the Song of Solomon), but because this gift, so powerful, flourishes in the security of commitment.

As for singleness, the Bible never presents it as a "failure": Jesus himself and Paul were single, and Paul sees in it a precious freedom to serve God. Married or single, your worth doesn't come from your status but from your identity as God's child. The essential, in both cases, is to live for God and to love where he has placed you.
items.evidence: Biblical teaching values marriage *and* singleness equally (1 Corinthians 7), contrary to cultures that devalue one or the other. Moreover, sociological studies regularly connect stable, faithful marital commitment to better well-being for spouses and children — consistent with the design described from Genesis onward.

items.q: How do I keep faith when life is routine or hard?
items.a:
Faith lived daily isn't made only of mountaintops: the real work happens in *ordinary* faithfulness, when nothing shines. And that's exactly where the Bible encourages you: "Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up." Constancy, not intensity, ripens you.

In routine, shift your gaze: "whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters." A mundane task done for God becomes worship; faithfulness in small things has value in his eyes. Seek his presence *within* the everyday, not just alongside it.

When it's hard or monotonous, lean on three things: the *disciplines* that feed you even without emotion (Word, prayer, community), the *remembrance* of what God has already done, and the *hope* of reward ("in due season"). Emotions come and go; faith holds by habit and will, not by feeling. Be faithful today — God uses gray seasons to root what easy seasons cannot produce.
items.evidence: Growth — spiritual as human — happens mostly through the constancy of "small" habits, not through peaks of emotion (2 Peter 1:5-8). Psychology of perseverance confirms this: it's the routines sustained through bland periods that produce, over time, the most solid transformations.

items.q: How do I know if I'm called to serve God / to ministry?
items.a:
Every believer is already called to serve God where they are — but you're probably asking whether you're called to a *particular ministry* (pastor, missionary, leader). Good news: God clarifies this calling to those who seek it, by bringing together several signs.

Look for four convergences. *Desire*: a deep, lasting draw to serve in this way ("if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task"). *Gift*: do you have abilities that God blesses and that build up others? *Fruit*: are lives actually touched when you serve? *Confirmation*: do mature leaders and your community recognize this calling in you? An inner calling not confirmed by the body of Christ calls for caution.

Add character: the Bible stresses *who you are* more than *what you do* (the criteria in 1 Timothy 3 are mostly life qualities). Don't rush ahead of God, but don't bury his call either: serve now in your church, take on simple responsibilities, and let the calling clarify and confirm itself over time. Often you discover your calling *by serving*, not by waiting for perfect certainty.
items.evidence: Biblical calling is discerned by convergence (inner desire *and* gift *and* fruit *and* community confirmation), never by feeling alone — which protects against illusory vocations. The priorities of 1 Timothy 3 focus first on character, reminding us that inner solidity comes before talent.

items.q: How do I live a holy life without falling into legalism?
items.a:
It's a delicate balance, and the Bible refuses both opposite traps. *Legalism* says "I'll be accepted if I keep enough rules" — it turns faith into performance and steals joy. On the flip side, *license* says "since I'm saved by grace, my life doesn't matter." Both miss the Gospel.

The key is *order*. You don't become holy to *be* loved by God; you walk in holiness *because* you're already loved and saved. "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free." Holiness isn't a prison of rules, but the normal, free life of a grateful child, led by the Spirit — not by fear.

In practice: keep your eyes on Jesus rather than a scorecard of "good points"; seek holiness of *heart* (motives, love) and not just appearances; obey out of gratitude, not to earn acceptance; and when you fall, return to grace without drowning in shame. "The grace of God teaches us to say no to ungodliness... and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives." True holiness sets you free and brings joy, never rigidity and anxiety.
items.evidence: The New Testament explicitly fights legalism (the letter to the Galatians in its entirety) while refusing license (Romans 6:1-2). This balance — obeying *from* gratitude rather than *to* earn — is recognized as psychologically healthier and more lasting than motivation by fear or guilt.

items.q: How do I overcome discouragement in serving?
items.a:
Discouragement threatens even the most zealous — Elijah, after an immense victory, wanted to die from exhaustion. So it's not a sign that you're "not made for this"; it's often a sign of burnout. And God, with Elijah, didn't start with a sermon: he made him sleep and eat, before speaking to him gently. Take care of your body and your soul; it's not anti-spiritual.

Then return to the source. You serve *Him*, not applause or immediate results: "it is the Lord Christ you serve." When you serve for approval or visible fruit, you exhaust yourself quickly; when you serve from love for him, you endure. Reconnect to his presence before taking action again.

Finally, don't carry everything alone: Elijah believed he was the last faithful one — he was wrong. Share, delegate, receive support, surround yourself. And keep your eyes on the eternal reward rather than on today's tally: "Let us not grow weary of doing good, for we will reap at the proper time, if we do not give up." Your faithfulness is never in vain in the Lord, even when you don't yet see its fruit.
items.evidence: The episode of Elijah (1 Kings 19) is remarkably modern: God addresses *physical* exhaustion (sleep, food) before spiritual discouragement. Modern burnout prevention recommends exactly this — rest, support, realistic expectations, purpose — confirming the wisdom of the account.

items.q: Does hell really exist? How can a God of love allow it?
items.a:
Surprisingly, it's Jesus, the gentlest of all, who spoke most of hell — not to frighten, but to warn out of love, like cautioning a child about real danger. Hell, at its heart, is the consequence of a final refusal of God: it's existing forever *far* from the source of all life, all good, and all love.

How can a God of love "allow" it? Because true love respects freedom. God doesn't force anyone to love him; if he imposed it, it would no longer be love. It's by respecting our choice to the end that he permits us to refuse him too. As C. S. Lewis said, the doors of hell are "locked from the inside."

But all of Scripture cries out that God doesn't want this for anyone: "he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance." He even gave everything — his own Son — to spare us from it. The cross is the exact measure of what God was willing to pay to keep you from this. Hell is not God's will for you: it's what he wants to save you from.
items.evidence: A God who leaves humans the freedom to reject him is actually more coherent with love than a God who would force love: forced love is not love. And Scripture's insistence that God "does not want" this loss (Ezekiel 33:11; 1 Timothy 2:4) rules out seeing him as cruel.

items.q: What happens to those who never heard about Jesus?
items.a:
This is one of the most sensitive questions, and Scripture answers it seriously without revealing everything. Two truths first. One: God is perfectly *just* — "will not the Judge of all the earth do right?" No one will be treated unfairly; no one will be condemned for refusing a message they never could have heard. Two: God is also perfectly *loving*, and "wants all people to be saved."

How to reconcile this? Scripture indicates that God already reveals himself to everyone, through creation ("the invisible qualities of God... are clearly seen in what has been made") and through moral conscience ("they show that the requirements of the law are written on their hearts"). Each person is therefore accountable for the light they have *received*. God judges hearts with an equity that we don't have.

What we *know* clearly: it is Jesus who saves, God's justice is perfect, and no one will be shortchanged. What we don't know — the precise fate of each individual — let's leave that to a Judge infinitely more just and good than we are. And rather than speculate, this question should *drive* us: since not all have heard, let us make known the love of God.
items.evidence: Scripture establishes that God holds each person accountable *to the measure of what they have received* (Luke 12:48; Romans 2), ruling out the idea of arbitrary condemnation. It affirms God's perfect justice without claiming to settle each individual case — an honest humility, preferable to simplistic answers in either direction.

items.q: Science and creation: do you have to choose between the Bible and evolution?
items.a:
No, you don't necessarily have to "choose": millions of believers, including many scientists, don't see a war here. The Bible and science often answer different questions: Genesis says *who* created and *why* (a personal God, with a purpose of love); science explores *how* and *when*. "Who" and "how" contradict each other no more than "the author of a book" and "the printing press that produced it."

On *how* to read Genesis, faithful Christians disagree in good faith: some read the "days" literally (recent creation), others see it as poetic language compatible with an ancient universe, still others believe God could have created *through* a process he directs. On these points, humility and mutual respect are called for — the essential isn't the mechanism, but the fact: it's God who's at the origin, and human beings have unique dignity, "created in his image."

What faith holds firmly: the universe is not purposeless chance, life has meaning, and humanity is not an accident but a being willed and loved. Whether God created in an instant or through a long process, he remains the Creator. Don't let a debate over the *how* pull you away from the *Who*.
items.evidence: Often-ignored fact: modern science was born in a Christian framework, carried forward by believers (Galileo, Kepler, Newton), and many great scientists today are believers (Francis Collins, human genome). Moreover, the idea of an *absolute beginning* to the universe (the "Big Bang") remarkably echoes Scripture's opening claim: "In the beginning…"

items.q: Why are there so many churches and different denominations?
items.a:
The diversity of churches is bewildering, it's true. But let's distinguish two things. On the *essential*, there is actually deep *unity*: almost all confess one triune God, Jesus true God and true man, dead and risen, salvation by grace, the authority of Scripture. "There is one body, one Lord, one faith." This common foundation is immense.

Differences concern mainly the *secondary*: forms of worship, organization, ways of baptizing, styles, cultural sensitivities. Part of this diversity is *healthy* — like one family with varied temperaments, or one Gospel expressed in a thousand cultures. Another part comes, sadly, from our sins: pride, quarrels, human divisions that Scripture itself deplores.

Don't let this discourage you. Look for a church *centered on Jesus and faithful to the Bible*, where God and people are loved — the "label" matters less than this reality. And remember Jesus's prayer "that they be one": unity doesn't mean uniformity, but love across differences. Focus on what unites, more than on what distinguishes.
items.evidence: Despite apparent dispersion, the major Christian denominations share a common doctrinal core, formulated in the early centuries (e.g., the Creed). The diversity of expressions, far from undermining faith, illustrates its unique capacity to incarnate itself in all cultures — present today in nearly every people on earth.

items.q: What does the Bible say about other spiritual practices (fortune-telling, horoscopes, occultism)?
items.a:
The Bible warns clearly: divination, fortune-telling, horoscopes, mediums, spiritism, occultism. "Let no one be found among you... who practices divination or sorcery... Anyone who does these things is detestable to the Lord." This isn't superstition in reverse: it's a matter of *source*. These practices seek to know the future or access power apart from God — and they open doors to what is not of him.

Why does God forbid it? Out of love, to protect you. On one hand, it turns you away from trust in him toward deceptive or evil powers; on the other, it promises false control over the future, when peace comes from entrusting the future to a Father who loves you. This isn't a harmless game, even "just for fun."

The good news: in Jesus, you don't *need* these things. God guides you safely through his Spirit and his Word, and he holds your future. If you've engaged with it, no shame: you can confess it, renounce it, and be set free in Jesus's name, who "disarmed the powers and authorities... triumphing over them by the cross." Turn to the true Source.
items.evidence: The biblical prohibition of occultism is constant, from Old Testament to New (Acts 19:19, where new believers burned their magic books). This isn't obscurantism but a protective warning: Scripture treats these practices as real and dangerous, not as mere folklore.

items.q: How should a Christian approach sensitive topics (sexuality, society) with love?
items.a:
On burning issues (sexuality, society, bioethics…), the Christian is called to hold together two things the world often opposes: "the truth *in* love." Neither abandon truth for a "love" that won't dare say anything, nor assert "truth" without love that wounds and pushes away. Jesus was "full of grace *and* truth" — both, at 100%.

A few guideposts. First, *humility*: we're all sinners saved by grace, never in a position of superiority ("first remove the plank from your own eye"). Next, *distinction* between person and issue: you love and respect unconditionally *each* person, created in God's image, even when you disagree on a topic. Jesus ate with those religion rejected, without giving up his convictions.

Finally, *tone and setting*: many debates are ruined by manner, not substance. Listen first, seek to understand, speak "with gentleness and respect," and remember your goal isn't to win an argument but to love a person toward God. Truth without love condemns; love without truth deceives; together, they look like Jesus.
items.evidence: "Full of grace and truth" (John 1:14) sums up Jesus's approach, never opposing the two: radical welcome of persons *and* candor about truth. This double faithfulness — refusing both rejection and relativism — is what makes a witness both credible and loving.

items.q: If God knew Adam would sin, why create him?
items.a:
This is a formidable and ancient objection. Let's reframe it: if God, who knows all things, foresaw the Fall, why create at all? The answer lies in the *nature of love and freedom*. God wanted beings capable of truly *loving* him — but love only makes sense if it's free. Creating free humans meant accepting the risk they'd turn away. Love that's programmed, with no possibility of refusal, would be mere mechanism, not relationship.

In other words, God judged that a world where true love is possible — with the risk of evil — was worth more than a world of puppets incapable of love. The freedom that makes the worst possible also makes the greatest possible: love, sacrifice, courage, forgiveness.

And God didn't create as a detached spectator: knowing the Fall, he had already planned the remedy. Scripture speaks of the Lamb "slain from the creation of the world": before even creating, God was resolved to come himself and pay the price to save us. He didn't create a problem he'd flee; he created a world he was resolved to redeem at his own cost.
items.evidence: The "paradox of free will" has been debated since antiquity: most philosophers acknowledge that authentic love requires freedom, thus the possibility of refusal. That God provided *from the beginning* the remedy (the plan of redemption, 1 Peter 1:20) shows a Creator who accepts the cost of the freedom he grants.

items.q: Isn't faith just a crutch for the weak?
items.a:
The accusation says: "faith reassures the weak who don't dare face reality." But it turns on itself easily. First, it says nothing about the *truth* of Christianity: that a belief comforts doesn't prove it false (love also comforts, and it's real), nor that it's true. The real question is: Did Jesus rise? Not: Is it reassuring?

Second, the facts contradict the cliché of the "weak." Christian faith has produced some of the most rigorous minds (Pascal, Newton) and the bravest characters: martyrs who chose death rather than deny, reformers who faced slavery and injustice at risk of their lives. Often it takes *more* courage to follow Jesus against the grain than to go along with the times.

Finally, the Gospel is not a flattering crutch: it starts by telling you an *uncomfortable* truth — that you're a sinner, incapable of saving yourself. This isn't what a mind seeking reassurance would invent. Faith isn't an escape from reality: it's facing reality — evil, death, your own wretchedness — with hope grounded in facts, not wishes.
items.evidence: The "religion is a crutch" argument (Freud, Marx) is a *genetic fallacy*: explaining *why* you believe says nothing about the *truth* of the belief. And it applies just as well to atheism (which could be said to spring from desire to escape all authority). The question remains open: do the facts — including the resurrection — hold up?

items.q: What will Jesus's return be like?
items.a:
The Bible describes Jesus's return as a *personal, visible, and glorious* event—the exact opposite of a quiet coming. The angels announced it at the Ascension: "This Jesus will return in the same way you have seen him go into heaven." His first coming was humble (a manger, to save); the second will be radiant (to reign and judge).

It will be *visible to all*: "he comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him." It will not be a hidden event or reserved for a few initiates, nor a mere "spiritual idea," but a fact that will impose itself on the entire world. It will mark the resurrection of the dead, the judgment, and the renewal of all things—"new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells."

On the *details* and *timing* (order of events, tribulation, millennium…), faithful Christians hold different interpretations, and it's better to stay humble about that. What is clear and sufficient is this: he *returns*, he will have the final word over evil, and he calls us not to speculate about dates, but to "watch"—to live ready, in faith and love.
items.evidence: Christ's return is one of the most constant expectations in Christianity, present from the very earliest writings (around 50 AD). Notably: Jesus explicitly refuses to give its date (Matthew 24:36), calling instead for watchfulness, not calculation—the opposite of the sensational predictions that humans regularly manufacture.

items.q: What is heaven / eternal life?
items.a:
Heaven is not the bland image of clouds and harps: it is life fully alive, in direct presence with God, cleansed of all evil. The Bible describes it mainly by what *will no longer be*: "he will wipe away every tear… death will be no more; there will be no more mourning, crying, or pain." Everything that damages life will be abolished.

At its heart is a *person*, not merely a place: "they will see his face." The supreme happiness is to be at last fully with God, the source of all joy—like endless reunion with the One we are made for. The Bible even speaks of a *renewed* earth ("new heavens and a new earth"), not a vague, disembodied beyond: a restored creation, where everything is finally as it should have been.

Eternal life is not only "after": it begins *already* when you know God ("eternal life is that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ"). It is not endless boredom, but life without tears—beautiful beyond all we can imagine: "things that eye has not seen… that God has prepared for those who love him."
items.evidence: Contrary to a stubborn cliché, Christian hope is not a disembodied "elsewhere": the Bible announces the resurrection *of the body* and a *renewed earth* (Romans 8:21; Revelation 21). This vision—the restoration of the real, not its abandonment—is far more concrete and full than the popular image of clouds.

items.q: Will I have a body after death? Will I see my believing loved ones again?
items.a:
Yes to both—and it is a surprisingly concrete hope. Christian faith does not promise merely a floating soul, but the *resurrection of the body*. As Jesus rose bodily (he could be touched, he ate with his disciples), those who belong to him will rise with a real body—but transformed: "sown in corruption, raised in incorruption… sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body." The same *you*, without disease, pain, or death.

Will you see your believing loved ones again? The Bible answers yes, clearly. Paul comforts the bereaved this way: "we will be *together* with the Lord; therefore encourage one another with these words." He presents reunion not as an uncertain dream, but as assured comfort. Relationships in Christ are not destroyed by death; they are suspended, then restored.

Until the resurrection, those who die in Christ are already "with the Lord"—"absent from the body, present with the Lord." The separation is real and painful, but temporary. Death is not a period for the believer: it is a comma, before a reunion that will never end.
items.evidence: *Bodily* resurrection radically distinguishes Christian hope from purely "spiritualist" visions: it rests on a fact—the empty tomb and a tangible risen Jesus (Luke 24:39). Paul makes it explicitly the foundation of believers' hope and their reunion (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18).

items.q: How can we know if we are in the "last days"?
items.a:
"The last days" are, in the biblical sense, the entire period from Jesus's first coming to his return—so we have been in them *since* the apostles ("in these last days, God has spoken to us through the Son"). The question "are we at the end?" runs through every generation, and Jesus answers it very soberly.

He gives "signs" (wars, disasters, apostasy, the gospel announced to all nations), but warns immediately: "yet this is not yet the end." He compares these signs to "birth pains": real, but not allowing us to calculate a date. Above all, he is categorical: "No one knows the day or the hour, not even the Son, but the Father alone." Any prediction with a specific date therefore contradicts Jesus directly.

His conclusion is not "calculate," but "watch": live each day ready, in faith and love, like a servant waiting for his master at any moment. Whether the return is near or far, the required attitude is the same—not fear or speculation, but faithfulness today. The right question is not "when?" but "am I ready?"
items.evidence: History is littered with failed predictions about "the end"—all contradicting Jesus's clear warning (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7). The New Testament places the "last days" from the first century onward (Hebrews 1:2; Acts 2:17), shifting the emphasis from calculation to daily watchfulness.

items.q: Will there be a judgment? What will I be judged on?
items.a:
Yes, the Bible is clear: there will be a judgment. "It is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment." Far from being an arbitrary threat, this is actually good news: it means that evil will not go unpunished, that injustices will finally be repaired, and that nothing done in darkness will be forgotten. A world *without* judgment would be a world without justice.

What will I be judged on? The Bible distinguishes. For the unbeliever, it is a matter of giving account of their life before a just God—"according to their works." But for one who is in Christ, the decisive question is already settled: "he does not come into judgment, he has passed from death to life." Jesus bore his condemnation at the cross; the believer does not appear as an accused facing ruin, but as a child whose debt is paid.

For the believer, there remains an evaluation of their life and faithfulness—not to determine salvation (secured by grace), but for reward. The stakes of judgment are decided *now*: are you in Christ? If so, you can face it with confidence, not terror, for your Judge is also your Savior.
items.evidence: The universal desire for justice (that evil not "escape" unpunished) finds in the final judgment a coherent answer: without it, injustice would have the last word. The biblical distinction—the believer "does not come into judgment" (John 5:24)—radically transforms perspective: fear gives way to assurance for one in Christ.

items.q: Should I fear the end of the world?
items.a:
For one in Christ, no—the end is not something to dread, it is a hope. "There is no fear in love; perfect love casts out fear." The believer does not await a catastrophe, but the *return of someone they love* and the restoration of all things. The "end of the world" is not an abyss, it is a door to "new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells."

Many fears come from sensational scenarios (movies, predictions) that are not the Bible's message. Jesus himself tells his disciples about upheavals: "Let not your hearts be troubled… lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near." The attitude asked of us is not panic, but confidence: God holds history, and he has already won.

That said, there is a healthy seriousness: the question "am I ready?" deserves an answer. True security is not knowing the date, but knowing the Savior. If you belong to him, you can live each day in peace, without anxiety about tomorrow—"neither death nor life… will be able to separate us from the love of God." The antidote to fear of the end is not information, it is relationship.
items.evidence: Anxiety about "the end of the world" is chiefly fed by sensational narratives, not by the biblical text, which calls for calm and hope (Luke 21:28). On the human level, the antidote to fear of death is recognized as meaning and hope—precisely what resurrection offers the believer.

items.q: If God exists, why are there wars?
items.a:
This is one of the most frequent objections—and yet the Bible places the cause of wars not in God, but in the human heart. "Where do wars come from? Don't they come from your desires?" Lust, pride, hunger for power, hatred: wars are born from misused human freedom, not from a God who would want them.

People often ask: "Why doesn't God stop them?" But have you thought it through to the end? To eliminate *all* war by force, God would have to eliminate human freedom—thus love, choice, humanity itself. He would have to make us puppets. Evil is the terrible price of genuine freedom, without which love would be impossible.

And God has not remained indifferent: he entered our violent world, became himself a victim of human hatred (tortured, executed), and works through his people for peace ("blessed are the peacemakers"). He has promised to end it definitively: one day, "they will not learn war anymore." Meanwhile, the real question turns back on us: what do *you* do with your freedom—for hatred, or for peace?
items.evidence: The objection assumes God should eliminate evil *without* eliminating freedom—which is contradictory. Notably: the great historical advances against slavery, for human rights, and humanitarian action have very often been driven by convictions rooted in faith (Wilberforce, chaplaincies, Christian NGOs).

items.q: Why is there so much suffering in the world if God exists?
items.a:
The amount of suffering in the world is a real weight, and faith does not minimize it. The Bible explains it through a double rupture. First, human freedom that does evil: a vast share of suffering (violence, injustice, preventable famines, exploitation) comes from humans, not God. Second, a world itself "broken," "subjected to futility," which "groans" awaiting its deliverance—hence disease and disaster.

What Christianity offers uniquely is not an explanation that would make pain acceptable from a distance, but a God who *enters into* suffering. In Jesus, he wept, bled, was crushed. He does not contemplate our pain from on high: he shared it to the end, at the cross. No other faith dares say that God himself suffered *for* and *with* us.

Finally, the story is not closed. Present suffering is real but *temporary*; God has promised to "wipe away every tear" and renew all things. And he wastes nothing: he can birth, even from our worst wounds, compassion and good. Suffering will not have the last word—love will.
items.evidence: Christianity is the only great religion where God himself suffers: the cross. This "answer" is not theoretical but existential—it has enabled countless people to walk through the unspeakable, not by explaining pain, but by knowing it was shared by God. This is what theologian John Stott emphasized: in the face of suffering, only the cross makes God "credible."

items.q: Why do innocent children suffer?
items.a:
The suffering of innocent children is perhaps the most unbearable of all—and we must look at it with tears, not cold theories. The Bible gives no explanation that would "justify" it; it instead asserts the infinite value of every child and God's anger at what wounds them. Jesus was indignant when children were kept from him and solemnly warned anyone who would cause one of them to stumble.

Where then does this evil come from? From a broken world and freedom abused—most suffering inflicted on children comes from adults, from unjust systems, from a sick world, never from a God who would want it. God is not the author of this evil; he is its declared enemy, and he weeps with the victims.

Two hopes, without minimizing anything. On one hand, God's particular tenderness toward the little ones: Jesus takes them in his arms, and the Bible hints that those who die young are welcomed into his grace. On the other hand, the promise of total justice and comfort: one day, "he will wipe away every tear," and all this evil will be repaired. Meanwhile, faith answers this cry not with reasoning, but with presence—that of a God who has also known the suffering of an innocent: his own.
items.evidence: Our very revulsion at a child's suffering assumes an absolute moral standard ("this *should not* be")—hard to ground in a universe without God, purely material and indifferent. Paradoxically, the indignation that seems to accuse God presupposes a sense of right and wrong that takes root only in him.

items.q: If God is good, why doesn't He stop evil right now?
items.a:
That's a sensible question: if God can stop evil, why wait? The Bible gives a reason that flips the perspective: "The Lord is patient toward you, not willing that any should perish." This "delay" isn't indifference—it's *mercy*. The day God stops *all* evil at once, He'll also have to judge *everything* that is evil… including in us. This delay is an open door so that everyone can still turn toward Him.

There's a trap in the demand to "stop evil *right now*": where would God draw the line? Major evil, minor evil? Other people's evil… or mine too? We want Him to stop the wicked, but be patient with us. His patience holds us all.

Finally, God *hasn't* chosen passivity: He already struck a decisive blow against evil at the cross, He acts today through His people, and He has set a time when evil will be finally banished. It's not "never," it's "not yet"—the age of grace. The real question becomes: Will you make use of this delay God is offering you?
items.evidence: The objection "why is God waiting?" turns back on itself: an immediate judgment of evil would spare no one. The Bible reframes this delay as a time of grace (2 Peter 3:9), not weakness—and church history shows a God already acting against evil through the conscience, justice, and love of those who follow Him.

items.q: What's the purpose of my life? What is the meaning of existence?
items.a:
The meaning of your life isn't found *in you* like a hidden treasure to dig out, but in a relationship: you were wanted, created, and loved by Someone, for something. "We are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand." You're not an accident of chance: you are intentional.

The Bible sums up the meaning of existence in a double relationship: *knowing God* and *loving*—God and others. Jesus says that all of life hangs on "love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself." This is where the emptiness is filled: we are made for God, and "our heart is restless until it rests in Him" (Augustine). Everything else—success, pleasures—leaves a hunger that only this relationship satisfies.

Practically, your life gains meaning when you receive it as a gift to live *for* God and *in service* to others, with the unique gifts He's entrusted to you. You don't have to *create* a meaning from nothing; you have to *discover* the one for which you were made, and answer it. Your life has an Author, a worth, and a destiny—start by asking Him: "Why did You create me, and what do You want to do through me?"
items.evidence: Research in psychology (notably around Viktor Frankl, survivor of the camps) shows that meaning—more than pleasure—is the most determining human need for endurance and flourishing. The Bible places this meaning in a relationship and a vocation received, responding precisely to what human experience demands.

items.q: Why do I feel empty even though I "have everything"?
items.a:
This emptiness despite "having it all" is actually one of the most revealing experiences—and the Bible named it 3,000 years ago. King Solomon, who possessed *everything* (wealth, pleasures, wisdom, glory), tried it all and concluded: "vanity of vanities… all is vanity," a "chasing after wind." Emptiness at the top isn't a failure: it's a signal.

Why this emptiness? Because "God has put eternity in the human heart." You carry within you a hunger for infinity that no finite thing can fill. It's like trying to fill a bottomless vase with drops: goods, achievements, pleasures are real but too small for the space in you. This emptiness isn't an anomaly—it's a *call*.

The good news is that this lack has an address. "You have made us for You, and our heart is restless until it rests in You" (Augustine). The emptiness is filled not by *more* things, but by the One you are made for. Jesus says: "I am the bread of life; he who comes to Me will never hunger." Your emptiness isn't your enemy: it's the compass pointing toward God.
items.evidence: The paradox of "having everything and feeling empty" is a recurring observation, even among people at the height of material success—what psychology links to the fact that goods and status provide pleasure that quickly dulls ("hedonic adaptation"). Ecclesiastes describes this mechanism exactly, millennia before its scientific formulation.

items.q: How do I find inner peace?
items.a:
The inner peace everyone seeks doesn't come first from calm circumstances (they're always changing), but from a relationship that holds despite the storms. Jesus distinguishes it clearly from worldly peace: "I give you My peace; I don't give it to you as the world gives." The world's peace depends on things going well; His remains even when everything falls apart.

Where does it come from? First from being *reconciled*: much of our deep restlessness comes from a break with God, with others, with ourselves. "Being justified by faith, we have peace with God." Restoring this peace *with* God opens the peace *of* God. Then it's cultivated: "cast all your cares on Him," replace worry with thankful prayer, and "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts."

Practically: lay down your burdens instead of carrying them, bring your mind back to the present ("sufficient for each day is its own trouble"), feed yourself with what is true and good, and stay connected to the Source. Inner peace isn't the absence of problems, but a *presence amid* the problems—God's presence, who "will keep him in perfect peace whose mind is fixed on You."
items.evidence: Biblical peace doesn't depend on circumstances but on a relationship—which brings it close to what research identifies as the true drivers of lasting well-being (meaning, deep relationships, gratitude, letting go) rather than external comfort. Prayer and gratitude, recommended by Paul (Philippians 4:6-8), are today associated with measurable stress reduction.

items.q: I'm afraid of death. What does faith say?
items.a:
The fear of death is universal and deeply human—the Bible doesn't mock it; it offers to disarm it at the root. For the one who is in Christ, death has changed its nature: it's no longer a wall, but a *passage*. Jesus passed through it and came back alive, opening a way: "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live."  

Where does this fear come from? Often from the unknown and the feeling that everything would end in nothingness. The Gospel answers both: death isn't the end ("absent from the body, present with the Lord"), and the unknown has a face—the face of a Father waiting for you. The Bible even says that Jesus came "to free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death."  

This doesn't eliminate all human apprehension, but it removes death's *sting*. Paul can challenge it: "O death, where is your victory?" The key isn't denying death, nor reassuring yourself with words, but knowing the One who conquered it. Prepare yourself not by piling up certainties about the hereafter, but by trusting yourself to the One waiting for you there: the best answer to the fear of dying is knowing *who* will welcome you on the other side.
items.evidence: The fear of death is recognized as a fundamental human anguish, which nothing material resolves durably. The hope of resurrection rests, by contrast, on a historical event—the empty tomb and the appearances of the Risen One—not on mere wishful thinking; this is what has allowed so many believers to face death with an astonishing peace, even the martyrs.

items.q: I feel alone. Is God really there?
items.a:
Loneliness is a very real pain, and feeling alone isn't a lack of faith. The Bible takes it seriously—God Himself said from the start: "it is not good for man to be alone." We are made for relationship, and this need is legitimate. But He offers two complementary answers.

First, a *presence* that never leaves you, even when you don't feel it. "Where can I go from Your Spirit?… If I take the wings of the dawn… even there Your hand will guide me." Jesus promises: "I am with you always." Even in an empty room at 3 a.m., you are not alone: God is there, He knows your name and counts your tears. Speak to Him about your loneliness, simply—it's already breaking isolation.

Second, God comforts very often *through* others. He "sets the lonely in families." Don't stay isolated: community (a church, a group) is one of the great remedies He planned. The loneliness you feel can become a door—toward deeper intimacy with God, and toward new bonds with those He places on your path. You are sought, known, and loved, today.
items.evidence: Chronic loneliness is today recognized as a major public health issue. The two remedies the Bible offers—a transcendent *presence* *and* belonging to a real community—overlap with what research identifies as protective: deep social connection and the feeling of being known and loved.

items.q: Do money and success really make you happy?
items.a:
Money and success bring real comforts—the Bible isn't naïve about this. But do they bring *happiness*, lasting happiness? Experience and Scripture say the same thing: no, not at depth. "What good is it for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul?" Jesus points to a hunger that success doesn't touch.

Why? Because these goods fill real but *finite* needs, while your heart has a thirst for the *infinite*—for meaning, love, eternity. This is Solomon's conclusion, the richest man of his time: everything tried, everything obtained, and yet "vanity, chasing after wind." Money is a good servant and a bad master: "those who desire to get rich fall into… many sorrows," not because it's bad, but because it promises a happiness it cannot deliver.

True happiness, the Bible places elsewhere: in a living relationship with God, in love given and received, in a life that has meaning and serves something greater than itself. "There is more happiness in giving than in receiving." You don't have to despise money or honest work; but don't place your heart there: that would be building your joy on sand. Seek first the One you are made for, and the rest will find its proper place.
items.evidence: Studies on happiness converge: beyond a certain threshold covering essential needs, more income barely increases life satisfaction ("hedonic adaptation"). What research identifies as durably fulfilling—deep relationships, meaning, generosity, gratitude—corresponds exactly with biblical priorities, stated long before modern surveys.

items.q: Can my life really change?
items.a:
Yes—and it's at the heart of the Gospel: God is a specialist in changes you thought impossible. "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." It's not about patching you up a little, but re-creating you from the inside.

Maybe you've tried to change by willpower alone, and relapsed—hence the discouragement. The difference is the *power* at work: you don't change alone, but by the Spirit of God who comes to live in you and transform your deepest desires, not just surface behaviors. "It is God who works in you to will and to act in order to fulfill His good purpose."

Two truths to hold together. Change is *real* and *certain* (God commits to it: "He who began a good work in you will complete it"), but often *gradual*: like a season turning, not a light switch. Don't judge direction by one bad day. Look instead at the trajectory, be patient, stay connected to the Source, and let Him do what willpower alone has never managed. The Bible and history are full of radically transformed lives—yours can be too.
items.evidence: Life transformations tied to faith (breaking free from addictions, violence, despair) are massively documented, then and now—so much so that they are a historical argument in themselves (see Q131). They show a change that goes beyond mere personal resolution: lasting, often radical, and attributed by those involved to a power beyond themselves.

items.q: Why pray, if God already knows everything?
items.a:
Good question, and it touches on the *meaning* of prayer. If God already knows everything — "your Father knows what you need before you ask him" — then prayer doesn't aim to *inform* him or *convince* him. Its purpose is *relational*: not to change God's mind, but to connect you to him and transform you.

Think of a good relationship: a child talks to their father not because the father knows nothing, but because speaking *weaves* the bond. Similarly, prayer isn't a vending machine of requests—it's communion. In praying, you learn to trust, to align your heart with his ("your will be done"), to receive his peace, to see your priorities shift. Often, it's not the situation that changes first—it's *you*.

Yet mysteriously, God has *chosen* to link our prayers to his action: "You do not have because you do not ask." Without making it a magic formula, the Bible affirms that prayer truly matters, that God answers it, and that he makes us partners in what he accomplishes. So we don't pray to inform an ignorant God, but to walk with a loving Father—and that changes everything.
items.evidence: The objection assumes prayer serves to "inform" or "persuade" God; but the Bible presents it first as relationship and transformation of the one praying (Matthew 6:8-9). This insight dissolves the paradox: as in any loving relationship, communication has value in itself, independent of information transmitted.

items.q: How do I know if my life has value?
items.a:
The value of your life is not something you must *produce* or *earn* through your achievements, usefulness, or others' approval—it's something *given* to you, and nothing can take it away. You were created "in the image of God": that gives you intrinsic dignity, before any accomplishment.

The strongest proof is the *price* God put on you. We measure something's value by what we're willing to pay for it: God gave his own Son for you. "You were redeemed… by the precious blood of Christ." In the eyes of the Creator of the universe, you're worth the life of his Son—that's no small thing, and it depends neither on your performance, your past, nor how you feel today.

So when a voice tells you "your life means nothing," know that it's lying. Jesus says the Father knows every hair on your head and doesn't lose sight of a single sparrow—"so do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows." Your value isn't measured by what you do, but by who created you and how much he loves you. Receive it as a fact, before seeking it in your results.
items.evidence: Grounding human worth in usefulness or performance makes it fragile (it collapses with failure, illness, aging). The Bible roots it elsewhere—in God's image and the price of the cross—which gives an *unconditional* dignity, historically the source of the very notion of equal and inalienable human rights.

items.q: Why does God let me go through trials?
items.a:
No one enjoys trials, and God takes no pleasure in your pain. But the Bible dares a surprising perspective: God, without *causing* evil, knows how to use it. "Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials… because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance." He wastes nothing you go through.

Why does he allow them, then? Several possible reasons—we don't need to understand everything. Trials *shape* you (they produce endurance, maturity, depth—"suffering produces perseverance, and perseverance produces character"), they *draw you closer* to God (you seek him differently in a storm than in calm), and they *enable you to comfort* others ("he comforts us… so that we can comfort those in any trouble"). Often, what a trial destroys is what you were leaning on wrongly.
