Two guarantees, whatever happens. You're never alone: "when you pass through the waters, I will be with you." And nothing is lost: "in all things God works for the good of those who love him." This doesn't make the trial *good* in itself, but it means it won't have the final word, and God can draw a good from it that you don't yet see. Hold on: the crossing has meaning and an end.
items.evidence: "Post-traumatic growth"—the fact that people emerge from grave trials with greater meaning, empathy, and strength—is a phenomenon studied in psychology. It echoes the biblical claim that trials, though not good in themselves, can produce endurance and maturity (Romans 5:3-4).

items.q: How do I truly receive forgiveness and forgive myself?
items.a:
There are two parts to your question, and the Bible says "yes" to both. First, *being* forgiven by God: it's complete, total, the moment you ask him. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." He doesn't forgive halfway: he "hurls all our iniquities into the depths of the sea," he removes them "as far as the east is from the west." No sin is too great for the cross.

Then comes the often hardest part: *forgiving yourself*. Many remain trapped in shame while God has already turned the page. But if God—the only one truly wronged by sin—declares you forgiven, refusing to accept it means placing yourself above his verdict. Clinging to guilt that God has erased isn't humility; it's not trusting his grace enough.

Practically: receive God's forgiveness as a fact (not a feeling); replace the voice of accusation with what God says—"there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus"; repair what can be repaired; and each time shame rises again, bring it to the cross rather than dwelling on it. You're not defined by the worst you've done, but by what Jesus did for you. What God has erased, you have the right—and the duty—to stop carrying.
items.evidence: The distinction guilt / shame (see Q74) clarifies this: to forgive yourself means letting God's *objective* verdict ("forgiven") outweigh the feeling. Therapeutic approaches to self-forgiveness follow this logic—accepting the forgiveness received and stopping self-punishment—with measurable effects on anxiety and depression.

items.q: Did Jesus really exist?
items.a:
Yes—and it's not even seriously debated by historians anymore. The existence of Jesus of Nazareth, preaching in Judea in the 1st century and crucified under Pontius Pilate, is accepted by the vast majority of scholars, believers or not. The "myth theory" (Jesus never existed) is a marginal position, rejected by scholarship.

Why this certainty? Because sources are numerous and *cross-referenced*. Inside: documents written within decades of the events, by witnesses or close to witnesses. Outside, non-Christian authors mention him: the Roman historian **Tacitus** (around 116) reports that "Christus" was executed by Pilate under Tiberius; the Jewish historian **Flavius Josephus** (around 93) speaks of Jesus and his death; **Pliny the Younger** describes Christians who "sang to Christ as to a god."

In short, denying Jesus' existence would require setting aside more evidence than we demand for other ancient figures accepted without question. The real question, then, isn't "did he exist?"—he existed—but "who was he?" That's where everything hinges.
items.evidence: Non-Christian sources from the 1st-2nd century attesting to Jesus: Tacitus (Annals, XV), Flavius Josephus (Jewish Antiquities), Pliny the Younger, Suetonius, the Talmud. For historian Bart Ehrman (himself agnostic), "Jesus certainly existed"—the opposite is a position that "virtually no scholar" supports.

items.q: Can we believe in the resurrection of Jesus?
items.a:
This is the decisive question, and it's addressed as a historical inquiry, not as a blind wager. We start with facts admitted by most historians (believers or not): Jesus died by crucifixion and was buried; his tomb was found empty; many witnesses claimed to have seen him alive; and these witnesses were radically transformed.

Then we must explain *these* facts. The theft of the body? Terrified disciples had neither the means nor the motive—and above all, you don't die a martyr for a corpse you hid yourself. Mass hallucination? It doesn't work that way: Paul speaks of over 500 witnesses *at once*, many still living and verifiable ("go and ask them"). The wrong tomb? The authorities would have needed only to produce the body to extinguish the movement—they never did.

The transformation of the witnesses is most troubling: defeated disciples become fearless preachers, ready to die for what they *saw*. You can die for a lie you believe is true; not for a lie you *know* is false. The resurrection remains, by far, the explanation that best accounts for all the data. It's not believing *despite* the facts, but *because* of them.
items.evidence: The "minimal facts" (Gary Habermas): death by crucifixion, empty tomb, appearances, conversions of skeptics (James, Paul). The creed cited by Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:3-7 is dated by scholars to the very earliest years after the crucifixion—far too early for a "legend." No natural explanation covers the whole picture as well as the resurrection.

items.q: Is the Bible historically reliable?
items.a:
The Bible isn't a "detached" book: it's anchored in real history—kings, peoples, cities, dates—which makes it *verifiable*, and therefore *falsifiable*. Yet when tested, it holds up remarkably well. Luke, for instance, presents himself as a historian who has "carefully investigated everything," and his geographical and political data (official titles, routes, customs) have proven remarkably accurate when verified.

Two assets distinguish it. First, its *transmission*: the New Testament is the best-attested ancient text, with thousands of very old manuscripts (see Q60)—we read what the authors actually wrote. Second, its *corroboration*: dozens of biblical persons, places, and events are confirmed by archaeology and outside sources (see Q126).

This doesn't "prove" every spiritual claim by itself, but it establishes something important: the Bible is a serious historical document, not a collection of vague legends. Its authors claim to report "what we have seen and heard," and the verifiable checks regularly vindicate them. A book trustworthy where we can verify it deserves to be heard where it surpasses us.
items.evidence: Archaeologist Sir William Ramsay, starting skeptical, concluded after inquiry that Luke is "a historian of the first rank." Many details once disputed (the existence of Pontius Pilate, King David, biblical cities) have since been confirmed—see Q126. The manuscript density of the New Testament is unequaled in antiquity.

items.q: Does archaeology confirm the Bible?
items.a:
Archaeology obviously can't "prove" God, but it impressively confirms the *historical framework* of the Bible—to the point that discoveries have silenced old objections. For a long time, skeptics denied the existence of certain biblical persons or peoples; archaeologists' picks proved them wrong, one after another.

A few striking examples. The **Tel Dan stele** (9th century BC) mentions the "house of David"—so we found traces of King David, whom some claimed was legendary. The **Pilate Stone** (discovered at Caesarea in 1961) confirms the existence and title of Pontius Pilate. The **Sennacherib Prism** recounts, from the Assyrian side, the siege of Jerusalem under Hezekiah described in the Bible. We could add King Ahab, the people of Israel (Merneptah Stele), dozens of cities, customs, and verified details.

The overall picture points one way: the more we dig, the more the biblical setting is confirmed. No major discovery has ever refuted a clear biblical fact; many have confirmed them. This doesn't replace faith, but it shows that faith rests on *real* history, not on a tale.
items.evidence: Key discoveries: Tel Dan stele ("house of David"), Pontius Pilate stone (Caesarea), Sennacherib Prism, Merneptah Stele (mention of "Israel"), Caiaphas inscription, pools of Bethesda and Siloam rediscovered in Jerusalem. Archaeologist Nelson Glueck noted that no find has ever contradicted a clear biblical datum.

items.q: Is there evidence for God's existence?
items.a:
You don't "prove" God like a theorem (see Q1), but there are solid *indices* pointing the same way—strands that many find more reasonable with God than without him. None is a mathematical proof; together, they carry weight.

Four major lines. *A beginning*: science now accepts that the universe had a beginning (Big Bang)—yet everything that begins has a cause; what "lit" the universe? *Fine-tuning*: the physical constants are adjusted with breathtaking precision to permit life; chance alone poorly explains such "harmony." *A moral law*: our conviction that cruelty is *truly* wrong assumes a reference beyond our opinions. *Consciousness and reason*: that matter should produce minds capable of truth and beauty remains an enigma in a purely material framework.

Add the universal "hunger for the infinite," and the historical fact of Jesus (see Q123-124), and the picture sharpens. But most of all, the best "proof" offered by the Bible isn't an argument: it's an encounter. "Seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart." The indices open the door; crossing the threshold is where you discover the One they point to.
items.evidence: The beginning of the universe (Big Bang cosmology), the fine-tuning of physical constants, the existence of objective moral law, and the emergence of consciousness are four pieces of evidence that many philosophers and scientists consider better explained by a Creator than by chance alone. Astrophysicist (and agnostic) Fred Hoyle spoke of an "intelligence" that had "tinkered" with physics.

items.q: Doesn't science contradict faith?
items.a:
No — and the idea of a "war" between them is a recent myth, contradicted by history (see Q9). Modern science was born in a Christian world, driven by the conviction that a rational God made an orderly universe, and therefore one we could study. Kepler, Newton, Pascal, Faraday, Mendel, Lemaître (the priest-physicist behind the Big Bang): believers *and* pioneers.

The key is that science and faith answer *different* questions, without stepping on each other. Science explores the *mechanisms* (how things work); faith illuminates *meaning and origin* (why there is something, and for what purpose). Asking science "Why does my life have meaning?" is like asking a microscope to measure justice: that's not its domain. The two complement each other instead of competing.

Moreover, some scientific advances *align with* the Bible: the idea of a universe that had a beginning ("In the beginning...") long troubled those who held to an eternal cosmos. Many believing scientists today see in the order and beauty of reality not a retreating God, but a Creator who allows Himself to be admired. The real conflict is not science versus faith, but two *philosophies* (materialist or theistic) interpreting the same facts.
items.evidence: The "conflict" between science and faith is a polemical construction of the 19th century, largely abandoned by historians of science (the so-called "conflict thesis"). Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, is the father of Big Bang theory; Francis Collins, a Christian, led the Human Genome Project. Science includes many leading believers.

items.q: Sodom and Gomorrah, the Flood... do these accounts have a real basis?
items.a:
These accounts are not mere moral fables: the Bible presents them as rooted in real places and events, and certain elements find concrete echoes. Take **Sodom and Gomorrah**: the Bible places them precisely in the region of the Dead Sea, and speaks of destruction by "fire and brimstone." Sites in that area (such as Tall el-Hammam, which is debated) show traces of sudden, violent destruction that some researchers link to this kind of account — the debate remains open, but the geographical anchor is real.

As for the **Flood**, a striking fact stands out: nearly all ancient civilizations (Mesopotamian, with the Epic of Gilgamesh, but also Indian, Chinese, Native American...) preserve the memory of a great flood from which one man and his family escaped in a vessel. Such convergence of traditions across all continents is hard to explain if no significant event lay behind it.

There remains a good method of reading (see Q61): distinguish the *fact* reported from the *literary genre* and the *message*. The Bible does not recount these episodes to satisfy our curiosity, but to say something about God, evil, and judgment. Whether we debate their scope or details, they rest on a real foundation and carry a meaning that concerns us all.
items.evidence: More than 250 cultures worldwide preserve a flood account with common motifs (warning, vessel, survivors) — a pattern many judge difficult to attribute to pure chance. For Sodom, the biblical location (the Jordan plain, near the Dead Sea) is geographically sound, and sites in the region bear traces of sudden destruction.

items.q: Is faith compatible with reason, or must we "believe without thinking"?
items.a:
Biblical faith has never asked us to "believe without thinking" — that's a caricature. God actually invites us to think: "Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord"; "love the Lord your God with all your *mind*"; "always be prepared to give an answer...for the hope that you have." The Bible values examination: the Bereans are commended for *examining* the Scriptures to see if what they were taught was true.

We must distinguish *faith* from *credulity*. Credulity believes without reason, or against reason. Biblical faith, on the other hand, is *founded trust*: you trust God because of what He has shown — creation, the history of Israel, and above all Jesus and His resurrection (verifiable facts; see Q123-124). It's the same kind of rational trust you extend to a proven friend, or that a scientist extends to the order of reality: grounded in evidence, then lived out.

Faith and reason are therefore not rivals, but partners: reason examines the foundations, faith builds on them to go further, where reason alone cannot prove everything (as in any relationship of love or trust). Many of history's greatest thinkers were believers. You don't have to *shut off* your intelligence to believe — in fact, solid faith is nourished by it.
items.evidence: The Bible explicitly commands critical examination (Acts 17:11, the Bereans; 1 Thessalonians 5:21, "test all things"). History of thought is marked by rigorous believers (Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, Pascal, Newton, Gödel). "Faith" (trust grounded in reasons) and "credulity" (believing without reason) are two distinct things, often wrongly confused.

items.q: How do you explain that people change radically through faith?
items.a:
It's one of the hardest arguments to dismiss, because it's *observable*: everywhere and throughout history, lives are radically transformed through faith in Jesus. People imprisoned by addictions, hatred, despair are freed from them; enemies reconcile; the dying find peace. "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation."

The first example is historical: **Paul**, a fierce persecutor who had Christians imprisoned and killed, becomes overnight the greatest herald of the Gospel — and dies for it. How do you explain such a turnaround except through a real encounter? Likewise, the disciples crushed after the cross become fearless witnesses (see Q124). And since then, history aligns with transformations: slave traders became abolitionists (John Newton, author of "Amazing Grace"), criminals became peacemakers, the despairing were restored to life.

Of course, a change of life doesn't "prove" doctrine by itself — other factors exist. But the scale, constancy, and *nature* of these transformations (often beyond what willpower alone produces) constitute serious evidence that a real power is at work. The best test remains personal: "Taste and see that the Lord is good." Millions have done so — and testify to it.
items.evidence: Transformations linked to conversion (freedom from addictions, from crime, reconciliations) are massively documented and often witnessed by third parties, even in hostile contexts. Paul's conversion, from persecutor to apostle at the cost of his life, remains a major historical case, difficult to explain by anything but a real encounter with the Risen Christ.
